title: Malachi 3:1–6
context: The LORD of Armies answers the people’s complaint, “Where is the God of justice?” (2:17), announcing, “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me,” and that “the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple.” The prophet then asks who can endure that day, for the coming one is like a refiner’s fire who will purify the sons of Levi, and the LORD promises to come near in judgment against sorcerers, adulterers, perjurers, and those who oppress workers, widows, orphans, and foreigners, ending, “For I, the LORD, don’t change; therefore you, sons of Jacob, are not consumed.” The Gospels apply the messenger to John the Baptist (Mark 1:2; Matt 11:10; Luke 7:27), which readers in both traditions name without merging the passages, and both read 3:6 as shared ground about God’s faithfulness to his covenant people.

verses.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me! The Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple. Behold, the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, is coming!” says the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me!” Arminian readers note that “the Lord” in the next line renders Adonai, a title meaning master.

The Gospels apply the messenger to John the Baptist (Mark 1:2; Matt 11:10; Luke 7:27).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hear the Gospels’ use and many identify “the messenger of the covenant” with the coming Lord himself, a reading held with care.

Shared ground: both traditions name the Gospel citations without merging them with Malachi’s setting, and agree the promise answers the people’s question in 2:17.

verses.text: “But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire, and like launderers’ soap;
verses.arminianNotes:
“But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears?” Arminian readers note that the longed-for coming brings testing as well as hope.

He is “like a refiner’s fire, and like launderers” soap.’
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the holiness of God’s coming, which no one can face apart from his cleansing.

Shared ground: both traditions read the images of fire and soap as purification rather than destruction for those who are refined.

verses.text: and he will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi, and refine them as gold and silver; and they shall offer to the LORD offerings in righteousness.
verses.arminianNotes:
The prophet says he “will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi.” Arminian readers note that the cleansing begins with the priests.

The goal is that they “offer to the LORD offerings in righteousness.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s refining work restoring true worship.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that God purifies his servants so that their service may be acceptable, a theme that answers the priests’ failures in chapters 1–2.

verses.text: Then the offering of Judah and Jerusalem will be pleasant to the LORD as in the days of old and as in ancient years.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then the offering of Judah and Jerusalem will be pleasant to the LORD as in the days of old.” Arminian readers note the restoration of acceptable worship.

The contrast is with the blemished offerings rebuked in 1:7–8.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see worship made pleasing by God’s own refining.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as hope that God’s people will again worship him rightly.

verses.text: I will come near to you to judgment. I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, against the adulterers, against the perjurers, and against those who oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow, and the fatherless, and who deprive the foreigner of justice, and don’t fear me,” says the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “I will come near to you to judgment. I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, against the adulterers, against the perjurers.” Arminian readers note that the list joins worship with justice.

The oppressed worker, widow, orphan, and foreigner are named.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s concern for the vulnerable as part of his holiness.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that those who “don’t fear me” show it in how they treat others, and that God answers the question of 2:17 by coming to judge.

verses.text: “For I, the LORD, don’t change; therefore you, sons of Jacob, are not consumed.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For I, the LORD, don’t change; therefore you, sons of Jacob, are not consumed.” Arminian readers note that the people survive because God remains faithful.

His call to return in 3:7 shows that his constancy invites response.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s unchanging character as the ground of his people’s preservation (cf. Num 23:19; Jas 1:17).

Shared ground: both traditions confess God’s faithfulness here, and how his constancy fits with language of relenting is treated in the existing boxes at 1 Samuel 15:29 and Jonah 3:10.
